plays.author: aeschylus
plays.title: Persians
plays.proposed_subject: A Persian king fleeing in his chariot before a Greek horseman, read by Heydemann as Alexander pursuing Darius (John's pick, 2026-10-09: Plate Picks 1-7Pa, Heydemann, Hallisches Winckelmannsprogramm 8 (1883), the upper band; 2026-10-12: drawn with PhotoCraft, titled as Heydemann reads it).
plays.credit: After the folding plate in H. Heydemann, Alexander der Grosse und Dareios Kodomannos auf unteritalischen Vasenbildern (Achtes Hallisches Winckelmannsprogramm, Halle, 1883), pp. 3-5, the upper band: a band of a large Apulian amphora from Ruvo, Naples, Museo Archeologico Nazionale (Heydemann's Naples catalogue no. 3220), attributed to the Darius Painter, c. 330-320 BC. Heydemann reads Alexander pursuing Darius III. Scan: Heidelberg University Library.
plays.license: Public domain (published 1883). Heidelberg University Library marks the volume with the Public Domain Mark 1.0 (IIIF manifest, checked 2026-10-10).
plays.crop: The whole upper band as the plate prints it: the horseman, the chariot and its four horses, the axe-man and the Greek with the shield, with the stars, the plants and the dotted ground line (John). Left out: the plate's other bands and the paper.
plays.alt_text: A Greek horseman charges with a levelled lance at a bearded king in a Persian cap and patterned sleeves, who flees in a four-horse chariot driven by a young charioteer and looks back holding out his hand; beyond the horses a Persian swings a battle-axe at a young Greek with a spear and a round shield; stars above, plants and a dotted ground line below
plays.shows: The play's subject in a later war: a Persian king beaten by Greeks, fleeing, in Persian dress. Heydemann (p. 5) reads Alexander routing Darius III Kodomannos at Issos and Arbela; a museum photograph's caption gives the same reading. Not a scene of the play, which is set at Susa after Salamis. John (2026-10-12): titled as Heydemann reads it.
plays.method: Contour plate, pen lines on cream paper with the dress patterns drawn and no black ground, from Heidelberg's largest scan; every image step run in PhotoCraft (photocraft-cli 0.2.0), numpy and scipy only combining its masks, measuring and laying in John's marks: the lines at half maximum at 3 x the plate's px, weight 0.8 plate px (John's choice); the shading finer than the scan resolves drawn evenly in its own kind (John): hatch as thin lines along each band inside its outlines, stipple as even dots; the figures' area by the sealed watershed with pockets of ground, the lance and spear fitted as shafts, the greave's paired strokes as single lines; clay on the dark theme, the field ornaments clay with no lines there (John); John's PhotoCraft marks over three rounds; traced at 6400 px tall so the panel's scrolls stay whole; tools/persians.py.
plays.result: Approved by John on the fourth pass, 2026-10-12, after a head test of the king (A/B of line weight), four rounds on the shading (even hatch along the bands, inside the outlines, denser stipple), his ground calls by number, and three rounds of his marks in PhotoCraft. About seven hours' work over three days, much of it whole-band runs of 11 minutes (one stalled for an hour when the Mac ran out of memory). No outside review; the credit checked against Heydemann's text (pp. 3-5, Heidelberg IIIF pages) and a museum photograph's caption (Bridgeman); no Trendall number or modern inventory number found.

plays.author: aeschylus
plays.title: Seven Against Thebes
plays.proposed_subject: Eriphyle walking ahead of the four-horse chariot of Amphiaraos (John's pick, 2026-10-05: sweep 2 code 02n, 'as proposed').
plays.credit: After the plate in E. Gerhard, Auserlesene griechische Vasenbilder II (Berlin, 1843), Taf. XCI, 'Eriphyle' (text pp. 29-30): an archaic black-figure hydria, drawn in the Roman art trade (present location not checked). The plate is unsigned. Scan: Heidelberg University Library.
plays.license: Public domain (published 1843). Heidelberg labels the scan with the Public Domain Mark 1.0 (page 0218, checked 2026-10-07).
plays.crop: The main picture whole: Eriphyle, veiled, walking right and looking back; the four horses with raised forelegs; the two armed men in the chariot behind their shields, their spears and the reins. Left out: the picture on the shoulder above (fights, as Gerhard says, of a meaning he could not fix), the band's edges and the ground line, which the feet and hooves stand on, and the inscriptions. The ground the figures close in (between the horses' legs, under the muzzles) stays open.
plays.alt_text: Eriphyle walking ahead of the four-horse chariot of Amphiaraos
plays.shows: Related to the play: Amphiaraos, one of the Seven, setting out against Thebes in his chariot, and his wife Eriphyle, who sent him to the war. Gerhard's reading, after a similar vase; the play's backstory, not its action.
plays.method: Coloured plate, black-figure: black silhouettes on the orange clay, with incised lines and added white. John chose the silhouette over an outline drawing from a test on Eriphyle's head and the lead horse's head (2026-10-07). The black is drawn solid; the incisions, hatching and dots open in it, found on the plate smoothed along each stroke so close strokes stay apart, at least 1.5 px wide; grain specks in the black dropped. The added white, printed about 8.5 px out of register, moved back into the shapes its black outlines give; the lines drawn on it (brow, eye, mouth, fingers) from the plate's dark paint and a ridge filter. Eriphyle's feet drawn on the plate's own contour lines, the dashed ones joined (tools/seven_feet.json). Her face and hands drawn on John's traces over 4x crops of the plate, registered back by SIFT (tools/seven_traces.json); the end of the pale band ahead of the lead horse closed with his line, so the band is reserved clay. The band's edges and the ground line measured. On the dark theme the figures stand on a 1.5 px clay rim and the incisions show clay. tools/seven.py.
plays.result: Approved by John, 2026-10-07 ('looks good. i approve.'), after a test of the two styles, more detail in the eye and faces ('the eye in particular'), and the feet redrawn with their broken lines joined. About three hours' work (07:47-09:44 and 13:25-13:44). Revised the same day on John's traces: the face (his profile, brow, eye and veil edge; the pupil he drew cut, 'let's cut the pupil'), the hands, and the band's end; the warriors' faces left as they were ('warriors looked fine'). Approved by John ('approved'); about an hour and a half (15:12-16:37).

plays.author: aeschylus
plays.title: Suppliant Women
plays.proposed_subject: Amymone, one of the Danaids, running, and her father Danaus (John's pick, 2026-10-05: sweep 2 code 03n, 'as proposed (Amymone and Danaus; cut off Poseidon)').
plays.credit: After the plate in C. Lenormant and J. de Witte, Élite des monuments céramographiques III (Paris, 1858), pl. XX (text p. 55): a Nola amphora, formerly in the Durand collection (Catalogue Durand no. 208), owned in 1858 by M. Paravey (present location not found). The plate is signed L. Petit, sc. Scan: Heidelberg University Library.
plays.license: Public domain (published 1858). Heidelberg labels the scan with the Public Domain Mark 1.0 (the volume's IIIF manifest, checked 2026-10-07; the viewer page sits behind a bot check).
plays.crop: Amymone and Danaus, whole, his staff to its foot. Left out: Poseidon, who pursues her from the left (his cloak, forearm, hand and sceptre come into the crop but touch neither figure; the toes of his front foot lay across her raised heel and are cut off along the line of her sole), the clay strip they stand on, and the black ground. On the vase Poseidon and Amymone are on the front and Danaus on the back; the plate sets them side by side.
plays.alt_text: Amymone running, and her father Danaus
plays.shows: Related to the play: Amymone is one of the Danaids, the chorus of the Suppliant Women, and Danaus, their father, is a character in it. Her flight from Poseidon is later myth, not the play's action. The names are the Élite's (p. 55).
plays.method: Coloured plate, red figures on black, printed sideways (turned upright first), as Hippolytus: the black ground gives the outline; the plate's own lines by local contrast, faint lines joined along their gaps and seven breaks in the print joined by hand; the hair solid inside the painter's reserved outline (followed along its light ridge), her fillet left open; her fingers found at less blur; the two dark bands on Danaus parted from the ground along the plate's faint clay lines; Poseidon's toes cut away along her sole; the plate's own line weight (0.15%; at the house weight her hem's border ran into the pleats); potrace. tools/suppliants_aesch.py.
plays.result: Approved by John on the first pass shown, 2026-10-07 ('Approved'). About 35 minutes' work, most of it on the hair, her hand and the bands on Danaus.

plays.author: aeschylus
plays.title: Prometheus Bound
plays.proposed_subject: Atlas holding up the sky and Prometheus bound to a column, the eagle at his chest (John's pick, 2026-10-08: Plate Picks 4-6Va; 2026-10-10: everything inside the border, the rings drawn, silhouette with the red as a wash).
plays.credit: After a photo by Daderot (Wikimedia Commons, public domain) of the Laconic Kylix with Prometheus and Atlas, attributed to the Arkesilas Painter, 560-550 BC, from Cerveteri; Vatican Museums, Museo Gregoriano Etrusco, Room XVIII, Cat. 16592.
plays.license: The photo: public domain (Daderot's own work, so marked on Wikimedia Commons; taken 2019-04-06). The cup: ancient. No licence carried.
plays.crop: The cup's tondo: everything painted inside the innermost border ring (Atlas with the sky, the eagle, Prometheus and his column, the snake, the blood, and below the ground line the capital between two lotus sprays), with the three border rings round it. Left out: the black band outside the rings.
plays.alt_text: A long-haired bearded man bends his knees under the sky he holds up; facing him, a bearded man bound to a column, an eagle at his chest and his blood falling; a snake behind the first man; below the ground line, a capital between two lotus sprays; three rings round the circle
plays.shows: The play's subject: Prometheus bound for giving fire to men; the eagle Hermes threatens at the end (1021 ff.); his brother Atlas, whom he pities, holding up the sky (347 ff.).
plays.method: Photo of a cup's tondo, black-figure, a silhouette as Hecuba (John's choice), the added red as a grey wash: the slant taken out in numpy/OpenCV (the tondo's ellipse mapped to a circle); the crack (a ring of filler round a glued-back piece) erased and each mask carried across it by a harmonic fill; every later image step in PhotoCraft (photocraft-cli 0.2.0: crop, enlargement, grey, the channels by the Channel Mixer, blurs, Motion Blur along the strokes, Minimum and Maximum), numpy only combining its masks: the clay gives the outline; the incisions redrawn as even centre lines, the feathers straight; the wing's red, the beard and the bands filled edge to edge (John); the ropes on John's centrelines with black separations; the border's three rings fitted as circles; John's marks from five PhotoCraft rounds (green a clay line, blue black, red the wash); the ribs his lines alone; clay ground in both themes (John); potrace. tools/prometheus.py.
plays.result: Approved by John on the eighth pass, 2026-10-12, after a style test and seven rounds (five with his marks in PhotoCraft). About seven hours over three days. No outside review; the credit checked against the Vatican Museums' page (Laconic Kylix with Prometheus and Atlas, Cat. 16592, 560-550 BC, Cerveteri); Stibbe's catalogue of Laconian painters not read.

plays.author: aeschylus
plays.title: Libation Bearers
plays.proposed_subject: Orestes killing Aegisthus on his throne, with Clytemnestra coming up with an axe and Electra (John's pick, 2026-10-05: sweep 2 code 06n, 'WHOLE frieze').
plays.status: Drawn 2026-10-07; approved by John, and chosen for the site (2026-10-07: 'this will be the plate we use for the site')
plays.credit: After the plate in E. Gerhard, Etruskische und kampanische Vasenbilder des Königlichen Museums zu Berlin (Berlin, 1843), Taf. XXIV (text pp. 35-37): a red-figure stamnos from Vulci, bought in Rome by Bunsen in 1832 (no. 1007 in Gerhard's Berlins antike Bildwerke), by the Copenhagen Painter (Beazley); formerly Berlin, Antikensammlung F 2184, now Moscow, Pushkin State Museum of Fine Arts (inv. АВ 3742; 6528.3 in the Beazley Archive, no. 202912). The plate is signed Lith u. Farbendruck v. L. Steffen in Berlin. Scan: Heidelberg University Library.
plays.license: Public domain (published 1843). Heidelberg labels the scan with the Public Domain Mark 1.0 (the volume's IIIF manifest, checked 2026-10-07; the viewer page sits behind a bot check).
plays.crop: The whole frieze: Clytemnestra with her axe, Orestes, Aegisthus on his throne with the footstool, Electra; the axe head kept whole where it reaches into the tongue band. Left out: the tongue band along the top and the meander along the bottom (cut along their edges), the names painted on the ground, the drawing of the vase's shape, the plate's number and signature. The black ground the group closes in stays open on the dark theme, and so does the ground printed dark brown under Aegisthus' jaw (John).
plays.alt_text: Orestes kills Aegisthus on his throne; Clytemnestra comes at him with an axe, and Electra stands at the right
plays.shows: The play's own action: in the Libation Bearers Orestes kills Aegisthus, then his mother, who calls for an axe (line 889). The vase sets the killers' family round the deed: Clytemnestra with the axe, Electra. The figures are named on the vase (the Beazley Archive: 'all named'); Gerhard reads the scene so (pp. 35-37).
plays.method: Coloured plate, red figures on black, one leaf photographed open: the scan is levelled first (the frame's four edges fitted, mapped to a rectangle by a Coons patch; up to 10 px). Then as Suppliant Women: the black ground gives the outline; the plate's own lines by local contrast, the faint glaze lines from the blue channel, breaks in the print joined where the plate prints a line across; faces, Electra's ringlets and Aegisthus' genitals at the paint's own width; the blood a wash in the line colour, the lines black through it; the plate's own line weight (0.11%). John corrected pass 1 in Photocraft (blue: ink to add; green: ink to remove), and his marks are laid in as drawn (tools/libation_bearers_marks.json). potrace. tools/libation_bearers.py.
plays.result: Approved by John, 2026-10-07 ('approved'), on the third pass: his corrections on pass 1 (57 places: eyes, curls, outlines, pleats, the bands on Clytemnestra's dress), two more he sent as screenshots (Electra's hair between the leaves of her wreath; the edge of Aegisthus' drape, an outline that had broken up in tracing, as about 20 others had), and the ground under Aegisthus' jaw left open on the dark theme. About four hours' work (09:17-11:31 and 15:03-16:45), most of it on the faint lines, the faces and his corrections.

plays.author: aeschylus
plays.title: Eumenides
plays.proposed_subject: Orestes at Delphi: the Pythia fleeing the temple, the Fury, Apollo, Orestes at the omphalos, Artemis with her hounds (John, 2026-10-12: the whole of Bötticher's 1859 plate, fig. 1, drawn with PhotoCraft; 'It's a great plate').
plays.credit: After Carl Bötticher's drawing (signed 'Gez. v. C. Boetticher') in C. Bötticher, Der Omphalos des Zeus zu Delphi (Neunzehntes Programm zum Winckelmannsfeste der Archäologischen Gesellschaft zu Berlin, Berlin, 1859), plate, fig. 1, itself copied from O. Jahn, Vasenbilder (Hamburg, 1839), Taf. I (Bötticher p. 15, note 66): an Apulian red-figure volute-krater, 4th century BC, attributed to the Black Fury Group (Trendall, RVAp 167.13); Naples, Museo Archeologico Nazionale 82270 (H 3249; Beazley Archive 9036827). Scan: Heidelberg University Library.
plays.license: Public domain (published 1859). Heidelberg University Library marks the volume with the Public Domain Mark 1.0 (IIIF manifest, checked 2026-10-12).
plays.crop: The whole of fig. 1 (John): the two outer Ionic columns, the rules along the top, the hanging shields, wreath and animal heads, the ground line, and all the figures with the tripods, the laver, the omphalos and the laurel. Left out: figs. 2-4 below (the omphalos and the temple plan) and the paper.
plays.alt_text: Inside the temple at Delphi: the old priestess flees with her hands raised beneath a black Fury holding a snake; Apollo strides forward with his arm stretched out; Orestes kneels with his sword at the omphalos, which is wrapped in a net of tassels, beside a laurel; Artemis stands with two spears and her hounds; Ionic columns, hanging shields and tripods
plays.shows: The play's opening: the Pythia comes out of the temple in terror at Orestes at the navel-stone and the sleeping Furies (Eumenides 34 ff.), Apollo defends his suppliant (64 ff.). Bötticher (p. 8) reads the scene as Apollo consecrating Orestes's sword before the vengeance, not the purification; the Beazley Archive describes Orestes in Delphi with Apollo, the old priestess, the black Erinys and Artemis with her dogs.
plays.method: Contour plate, pen lines on paper with no black ground, from Heidelberg's scan (the Munich copy, MDZ bsb10221820, is larger but softer; Jahn's own plate in the Reinach library PDF is smaller), levelled by 0.43 degrees; every image step in PhotoCraft (photocraft-cli 0.2.0) but the levelling, numpy only combining its masks: the lines at half maximum at 4 x the scan's px, the plate's own weight (1.2 scan px, John); the faces, the omphalos net and its tassels found finer and traced at their printed width ('crisp, detailed', John); the field the columns and rules close marked ground, the spears fitted as shafts, the laurel's leaves, Apollo's latticed boot and Orestes's blade clay; clay on the dark theme, the Fury and the other black areas solid with a clay rim 3 scan px wide (John); John's marks in PhotoCraft (tools/eumenides_marks_1.png); potrace. tools/eumenides.py, which also cuts the Pythia for the Aeschylus home page.
plays.result: Approved by John on the third pass, 2026-10-12, after a style test (the whole plate, the plate's own weight), one round of his PhotoCraft marks (55 places: joins, faint lines, the two redrawn eyes) and a missed tassel he flagged. About two hours and fifty minutes. No outside review; the credit checked against Bötticher's text (MDZ OCR, pp. 8 and 15) and the Beazley Archive (vase 9036827: Naples 3249, earlier 82270 and H3249; Trendall, RVAp 167.13; FR pls. 179-180).

plays.author: sophocles
plays.title: Ajax
plays.proposed_subject: Ajax carrying the body of Achilles (John's pick, 2026-10-05: sweep 2 code 08n, 'WHOLE panel'). Drawn with PhotoCraft.
plays.credit: After the plate in E. Gerhard, Auserlesene griechische Vasenbilder III (Berlin, 1847), Taf. CCXI-CCXII, 4 (text pp. 124-125): a black-figure belly amphora from Cerveteri, Leagros Group, c. 525-500 BC, now Vatican, Museo Gregoriano Etrusco 16444. Scan: New York Public Library copy (HathiTrust).
plays.license: Public domain (published 1847). HathiTrust's rights code for the scan: pd-us-google (public domain in the US, digitized by Google). Heidelberg's scan, used to fill a torn strip, carries the Public Domain Mark 1.0.
plays.crop: The whole picture: Phoenix, Briseis, Ajax with the body of Achilles, the hoplite with the three-legs shield, the archer. Left out: the palmette band (except where the shield on Achilles' back rises into it, as printed), the frame, the ground stripe, the painted letters and the plate's numbers. The copyist's second hand of Briseis (in outline, under her raised white hand) is left out: on the vase she has one hand (John, 2026-10-09).
plays.alt_text: Ajax carries the armed body of Achilles; Briseis lays her hand on his helmet, the old Phoenix raises his hand, and a hoplite and an archer follow
plays.shows: Related to the play: Ajax, before the play, carrying Achilles' body out of the battle, the deed that made him claim Achilles' armour; the armour's award to Odysseus drives the play. The scene is the myth's, not the play's action. The names (Phoenix, Briseis, Diomedes, Teucer) are Gerhard's; the Beazley Archive calls them old man, woman, warrior and archer.
plays.method: Coloured plate, black figures on clay, a silhouette as Seven Against Thebes (John's choice from a test both ways), every image step in PhotoCraft: the sheet levelled from the frame's edges, a torn strip filled from Heidelberg's scan; the black solid, incisions and lines redrawn along smoothed centres, the hatched rims as straight strokes along each band's angle, the added white outlined on its printed line; John's marks laid in as drawn; potrace
plays.result: Approved by John on the fourth pass, 2026-10-09, after a whole pass marked in PhotoCraft, fourteen ground pockets and the fold's specks circled, Phoenix's nose, and the phantom hand removed. About a day's work over two days. No outside review; the credit checked against Gerhard's text (pp. 124-125), the Beazley Archive (302090, which cites the plate) and photos of the vase (ArchaiOptix, Wikimedia Commons, which give the inventory number 16444). Gerhard's text puts the vase in Munich, from the Candelori collection; it is in the Vatican.

plays.author: sophocles
plays.title: Antigone
plays.proposed_subject: Antigone with her hands bound, brought before Creon (John, 2026-10-02)
plays.status: Redrawn 2026-10-09/10 with PhotoCraft; approved by John
plays.credit: After the Apulian red-figure amphora of Panathenaic shape by the Darius Painter, c. 350-320 BCE, from Ceglie del Campo, Berlin, Antikensammlung F 3240 (RVAp 18/23), body A, upper frieze: Antigone with her hands bound, led by a guard, before Heracles and Creon. Photograph: ArchaiOptix (Commons file _04; files _05 and _06 used only to fit the vase's shape). Drawing traced from the photograph and changed.
plays.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (photos by ArchaiOptix; Commons file pages checked 2026-10-02). The drawing is a derivative and is released under CC BY-SA 4.0 with this credit. The file pages add that some museums permit photography for non-commercial use only; that is a note, not a licence term.
plays.crop: Antigone alone, cut along her own outline: the guard and his spear, the boy, Heracles and Creon left out; the guard's cord, which only touches her wrists, goes with him. Both feet kept, the back one half under her hem. Two mended breaks (across her upper arm and across her skirt) are erased whole; the folds they broke are joined across, on the arm along John's own trace. Unchanged in the 2026-10-09/10 redraw.
plays.alt_text: Antigone, veiled, her hands bound behind her back, her head bowed
plays.shows: The play itself: Antigone brought before Creon after burying Polynices (Antigone 384 ff.), as the vase is usually read. Some scholars connect the vase with a lost Euripidean Antigone, in which Heracles intercedes for her; John ruled (2026-10-02) that the image goes to Sophocles' Antigone whatever play the vase was painted for.
plays.method: Made with PhotoCraft (tools/antigone.py, 2026-10-09/10; the first tool, 2026-10-02/03, is in git history). Kept as approved: the fitted vase and its flat (tools/vase_unroll.py; photos 04, 05 and 06, focal lengths from EXIF), the cut, and John's 2026-10-02 traces of her hands, face and the folds across the arm mend (tools/antigone_traces.json). Every image step in PhotoCraft: the crop, grey, the clay map (red less blue), blurs, Maximum and Minimum (local contrast), thresholds. Painted lines along their centres, redrawn as clean even strokes, breaks from wear and the two mends joined; the veil's front lines placed by hand; the white streaks by her elbows not taken for glaze. Then John's corrections to pass 1, marked in PhotoCraft over the photo with pass 1 in red (blue to add, green to remove; tools/antigone_marks_1.png, on the tool's grid): the veil and the dark hair under it, her profile, eye and brow, nose, chin and neck, both hands and the belt redrawn by him, drawn as he drew them; her area follows his new profile; small holes in her closed (the eye no longer dark in dark mode). potrace.
plays.result: Redrawn with PhotoCraft and approved by John 2026-10-10 after two passes: pass 1, then his corrections marked over it in PhotoCraft in four sittings (the last three on the nose, chin, neck, eye and brow). His asks during pass 1: "distinguish between cracks and damage from the actual painted lines"; "we want these ink strokes to be clean, not cracked or jagged." His marks settle the old open question of the jaw: it is one line now. No outside review.

plays.author: sophocles
plays.title: Women of Trachis
plays.proposed_subject: Herakles and Deianeira with their infant son Hyllos, between Athena and Deianeira's father Oineus, all named on the vase (John's pick, 2026-10-05: sweep 2 code 09n; 'Don't worry about the nudity').
plays.credit: After the plate in E. Gerhard, Auserlesene griechische Vasenbilder II (Berlin, 1843), Taf. CXVI, 'Herakles und Hyllos' (text pp. 114-120): a red-figure pelike 'of Nolan style', formerly in the Durand collection (no. 318), bought at the Durand sale by W. Hope (present location not checked). The plate is unsigned. Scan: Heidelberg University Library.
plays.license: Public domain (published 1843). Heidelberg labels the scan with the Public Domain Mark (page 0241, checked 2026-10-07).
plays.crop: Athena, Herakles, Deianeira with the infant Hyllos across their arms, and Oineus, whole: Athena's crest and spear head where they rise through the palmette band to the rim, and her sleeve where it hangs over the left border. Left out: the palmette band, the meander band and the left border, the band's ornament seen through the crest's base (John, 2026-10-07), and the inscriptions. The black ground the figures close in stays open.
plays.alt_text: Herakles and Deianeira with their son Hyllos, between Athena and Oineus
plays.shows: The play's own people: Deianeira, Herakles and their son Hyllos, with her father Oineus and Athena, each named on the vase. A family scene before the play (Gerhard reads it as the child shown to his father and named), not its action.
plays.method: Coloured plate, red figures on a black ground, as Hippolytus: the black ground gives the outline; where Athena crosses the bands (crest, spear head, sleeve), cut along the plate's own lines. The lines are the plate's own paint (darker than grey 115) and its thin brown lines by a ridge filter, at least 1.5 px wide, the outline 1.5 px; the crest's dotted holder built as the plate draws it, outline and dots; the band's ornament inside the crest's base taken out, the crest's stalk and the helmet's top line redrawn through their centres. Traced as drawn, at the plate's own weight (0.104%); on the dark theme everything outside the figures stays open. tools/trachiniae.py.
plays.result: Approved by John, 2026-10-07 ('It looks pretty good'), on the third pass: the first, drawn by local contrast as Hippolytus, was 'too blotchy', so the lines were taken from the plate's own paint; then the band's ornament came out of the crest's base at his request. About two hours' work (00:00-01:31 and 06:31-07:09).

plays.author: sophocles
plays.title: Oedipus Tyrannus
plays.proposed_subject: Oedipus from the Syracuse krater, read as a scene from the play (the messenger's news); chosen by John 2026-10-02 over the Sphinx scene, which the play only alludes to.
plays.credit: After the Sicilian red-figure calyx-krater attributed to the Capodarso Painter, c. 330-320 BCE, Syracuse, Museo Archeologico Regionale "Paolo Orsi" 66557 (excavated at Syracuse, 1968-69); drawn from Dan Diffendale's photograph (Rome, Ara Pacis exhibition, 2024) and changed: cut out, cracks removed, staff redrawn as a straight rod, hair and beard drawn solid, hand redrawn, redrawn as line.
plays.license: Source photo CC BY-NC-SA 2.0 (Flickr licence of the exact file, checked 2026-10-02). The drawing traces only the ancient painting, which is public domain, so it does not carry the photo's licence (John, 2026-10-02: the vase's image is not copyrighted even if the photo is); the photo is credited.
plays.crop: Oedipus alone, cut out of the scene. Left out: the old messenger and the boy at left, the girl and the column at right, Jocasta, the stage floor, and the modern plaster fill by his elbow.
plays.alt_text: Oedipus, bearded, in a long embroidered robe, his hand at his beard, holding a staff
plays.shows: The play itself, as usually read (Taplin, Pots and Plays no. 22): the moment the Corinthian messenger's news lands, with Jocasta and the daughters beside him.
plays.method: Red-figure photo: a loose cut through the glaze (wide glaze joined to the background is left out), hand-drawn zones for the stage floor, the plaster fill, his shoes, and his head; three cracks erased and the lines they broke rejoined; a fourth crack, mended with grey plaster beside his hand, erased whole along John's outline of it, with nothing drawn along it: the lines it broke are joined across it (his hand's edges after John's trace, his robe's folds carried to his sleeve). It was first drawn as the staff, then as the edge of his sleeve; John, 2026-10-02: 'it looks like damage to the vase', 'The outlines of the crack need to be gone', 'Draw the lines so as to fill in the parts missing due to the crack'; below his sleeve the flaked staff redrawn as a straight rod on its painted centre line. Head revised after John's review (2026-10-02, 'crude and not refined'): the hair, a mass of tiny curls, drawn solid with its curly outline; the beard, whose strokes are too dense to hold apart at the house line weight, drawn solid with its long clay strands kept as light lines (John asked for a fuller beard); his hand at his beard redrawn stroke by stroke after John's trace of it (each stroke on a painted line read from Diffendale's second, sharper photo, or on John's trace where the paint is worn or under the restored patches), each finger a closed outline along its painted edges, with the black ground between two fingertips filled (John: 'Get the outlines. It's a line drawing'); the face lines redrawn as even lines along their centres. Lines by local contrast; painted lines broken by wear joined across their gaps where two line ends face each other (John: 'fill in the gaps of the lines where damage has erased parts'); more worn folds joined by hand, each checked against the photo (John: 'Do the folds but not hem and shoes'), and folds of the lower robe worn to faint dashes carried on where the photo still shows the dashes (found with a ridge filter, each checked by eye); the long crack across his robe re-placed onto the crack itself, whose dark line had been traced as a fold; the edge of his forearm drawn down from the wrist across the crack after John's trace; house line weight; potrace. tools/oedipus_syracuse.py.
plays.result: Usable. Revised: hair and beard solid, face lines even, the hand redrawn after John's trace with every finger outlined, the mended crack beside it gone, and lines broken by wear joined. The robe folds are sharp; the hem and the shoes are worn on the vase and stay rough; the shoes are drawn as solid black shapes.

plays.title: Electra
plays.proposed_subject: Orestes brings Electra the urn of his supposed ashes, Pylades behind him (John's pick, 2026-10-09: Plate Picks 10-7Ba, Laborde, Vases Lamberg I pl. VIII; 2026-10-10: drawn with PhotoCraft, titled with the scene).
plays.credit: After the plate in A. de Laborde, Collection des vases grecs de M. le comte de Lamberg I (Paris, 1813), pl. VIII (text pp. 8-10): a South Italian red-figure bell krater attributed to the Sydney Painter, about 350 BC, Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna, Antikensammlung IV 689 (from the Lamberg collection, bought 1815). Scan: Heidelberg University Library.
plays.license: Public domain (published 1813). Heidelberg labels the scan with the Public Domain Mark 1.0 (the volume's IIIF manifest, checked 2026-10-10).
plays.crop: The three figures, as the plate prints them. Left out: the dark ground, the panel's frame and the meander band below.
plays.alt_text: A young man in a short cloak holds out a two-handled urn to a veiled woman, who raises a hand to her chin; behind him a second young man in a cloak stands with two spears, his hand on his hip
plays.shows: The play itself: Orestes, in disguise, brings Electra the urn said to hold his ashes (Soph. El. 1098-1226). Laborde (pp. 8-10) ties the scene to those lines and quotes them; the museum names the figures Pylades, Orestes and Electra. Laborde says the vase was found at Avella. John (2026-10-10): titled with the scene.
plays.method: Colour aquatint, red figures on a dark ground with the interior lines drawn: the panel squared (its four edges fitted as lines and the corners mapped to a rectangle); every image step run in PhotoCraft (photocraft-cli 0.2.0), numpy only combining its masks and measuring: the dark ground gives the figures' area, with five pockets of ground opened (inside Pylades' arm, under his arch, at Orestes' waist, by the urn's foot, between Electra's feet); the cut follows the top of the clay band the figures stand on, measured in every column, and the soles close along it (John); Pylades' eye drawn on points read off the plate; grain specks dropped; every outline drawn on the dark ground outside the clay; the line weight kept at pass 1's; tools/electra_soph.py.
plays.result: Approved by John on the second pass, 2026-10-10, after his note on pass 1 that the toes were open below. About an hour and a half's work, the credit included. No outside review; the credit checked against Laborde's text (pp. 8-10) and the Kunsthistorisches Museum's record (IV 689).

Photographs: Marie-Lan Nguyen, 2011 (Commons), and the Metropolitan Museum of Art (Open Access, DP165159 and DP165160). Drawing traced from the photographs and changed.
plays.license: Nguyen's photo CC BY 2.5 (Commons file page, checked 2026-10-03); the Met's photos CC0 (Open Access; the object record says isPublicDomain: true). The drawing traces only the ancient painting, which is public domain, so it carries no licence (John's ruling on Oedipus Tyrannus, 2026-10-02; on this drawing, 2026-10-03: 'Don't care about license'); the photographers are credited.
plays.crop: Philoctetes with the rock he sits on, his bow case and the tree, cut out as one (John, 2026-10-03: 'include quiver and bow and the rock'; 2026-10-09: 'Can we also add the tree? I think it completes the framing nicely'). The tree whole: trunk, stub branch and both boughs; the left bough ends where the photo's view of the vase runs out. The black ground seen through the scene stays open (the two gaps between his legs drawn black on the light page too). Changed in the 2026-10-09 redraw: the tree added; the rock's brown washes drawn as its brushstrokes (John: 'duplicate the texture brush strokes on the rock'); hair, beard and the black top of the head as layered brushstrokes, with no outline round the top and back of the head; the dark band round the hanging foot as a wash.
plays.alt_text: Philoctetes alone on Lemnos, seated on a rock under a tree, his bandaged leg drawn up, his bow case beside him
plays.shows: The play itself: Philoctetes alone on Lemnos with his wound and the bow, where the Greeks left him, the situation the play opens on. Not a myth the play only mentions.
plays.method: Made with PhotoCraft (tools/philoctetes.py, 2026-10-09; the first tool, 2026-10-03, is in git history). Kept from the first drawing as approved: the vase's profile and the cameras of the three photos fitted together (tools/vase_unroll.py), the flat over the scene (within 3% of the vase's lengths), Nguyen's photo in the middle and the Met's DP165159 toward the sides, and the cut-out's hand-placed points. Every image step in PhotoCraft: grey, red less blue (Channel Mixer), blurs, Maximum and Minimum (local contrast, and the clay level round each pixel). Painted lines by local contrast, drawn along their centres at the paint's own width, smoothed along the line, breaks joined; the line weight pinned at 0.21%. His brow, eye and pupil at the paint's own shape (from the Met photo where Nguyen's has glare). Hair and beard: the brown paint as a soft stepped tone with the curl strokes sharp on it, darker toward the black top of the head and in the goatee; the black top as very dark layered strokes from the Met photo; the curls' edge against the ground in the tone, and no outline round the top and back of the head. The dark band round the hanging foot, and the rock's brown brushstrokes, as stepped washes following the paint. The tree from a flat of its own (its boughs run onto the vase's shoulder, outside the scene's flat), laid onto the frame by the similarity that fits the two flats along the seam where the trunk meets the rock (0.65 px median); photo DP165159. John's 2026-10-03 traces of the head, feet and hands kept as a check (tools/philoctetes_traces.json, --traces). Washes as paths of class tone; potrace.
plays.result: Redrawn with PhotoCraft 2026-10-09 and approved by John after five passes and two rounds on the hair. His asks: the hair and beard as brushstrokes ('similar to how we did hair in other plates'), of four treatments the brown paint alone in steps ('D, but note the different dark and light intensities'); 'the shadow around his foot needs some correcting' (the hanging foot's band, now a wash); the rock's brushstrokes; no outline round the head ('the white buffer with black line outlining the head doesn't work'); the black top as 'VERY dark layered brushstrokes so all the hair is same'; the hair darker toward the top, the goatee darker; 'More blending of tones'; the tree; then, of three layerings, the soft tone with the most curl strokes.

plays.author: sophocles
plays.title: Oedipus at Colonus
plays.proposed_subject: Blind Oedipus at the altar between his daughters, Ismene and Antigone, from the Apulian krater Taplin reads as a scene from the play (Pots & Plays no. 27); the three on the altar chosen by John 2026-10-02, over Oedipus alone.
plays.status: Redrawn 2026-10-10 with PhotoCraft; approved by John
plays.credit: After the Apulian red-figure calyx-krater close to the De Schulthess Painter, 340s BCE, formerly Melbourne, Graham Geddes collection A 5:8; drawn from the photographs in J. R. Green, Ancient Voices, Modern Echoes: Theatre in the Greek World (Nicholson Museum, University of Sydney, 2003), pp. 4, 26 and 29 (HathiTrust mdp.39015060089391), with the painted lines and borders outside p. 26 (Ismene, the altar's left end, the strip along the bottom) from a photo of the scene found online (source unknown), placed on the same photo as reprinted in Oliver Taplin, Pots & Plays (Getty, 2007), no. 27, p. 101 ("From Green 2003, p. 4"), checked against the photo in Digital LIMC (monument 8378, photo 8569X101, © Graham Geddes Collection (once)), and changed: cut out, columns and tripods left out, redrawn as line, the daughters' faces, Antigone's hand and forearm, and Oedipus' lower fingers drawn after John Boyer's traces and marks.
plays.license: The found photo's source and terms are unknown (John, 2026-10-03: "don't worry about the credit"). The other source photos are in copyright: Green 2003 (the HathiTrust scan is under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0), its reprint in Taplin 2007, and the Digital LIMC photo (CC BY-NC 4.0 on the LIMC site). The drawing traces only the ancient painting, which is public domain, so it carries no licence from any of them (John, 2026-10-02: "The vase's image ISN'T copyrighted even if the photo IS"; the Syracuse drawing set the same rule for a CC BY-NC-SA photo); the photos are credited.
plays.crop: Oedipus seated on the altar between Ismene (left) and Antigone (right), with the altar, cut out of the scene. Left out: the two Ionic columns behind the altar and their tripods, the bearded king at far left (Creon for Taplin), the youth at far right (Polynices), the Erinys above, the boukranion, platters and festoons. Unchanged in the 2026-10-10 redraw; the band with white ribs over Ismene's head and down behind her neck is drawn as a headdress, not hair (John, 2026-10-10: 'This is not part of hair but some crown or some attire').
plays.alt_text: Blind Oedipus, white-haired and bearded, seated at an altar with his staff, one hand raised, between his daughters Ismene and Antigone
plays.source_file: Drawn from: HathiTrust mdp.39015060089391 (Green 2003), page images seq 6 (p. 4, the whole vase, 1.8 times the plate's scale), seq 28 (p. 26, the right half of the scene, 6.4 times) and seq 31 (p. 29, Oedipus' head and hand, 12.8 times), TIFF, downloaded by John (2026-10-03): https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=mdp.39015060089391. Ismene's lines: a 547x560 photo of the scene John found online (2026-10-03; probably from a Facebook post, source unknown; kept locally as found.png), registered to the plate (SIFT, median error 0.42 of its px; local misfit over Ismene 0.1 plate px). Frame: https://media.getty.edu/Text/6f3674dd-413a-56da-bec2-9da5564907df.pdf, page 112 (book p. 101), the plate, a 942x641 JPEG at 150 dpi (pdfimages -j -f 112 -l 112); every hand-placed point is in its px. Checked against: Digital LIMC, monument 8378 (scene 8569), photo 8569X101, the whole vase in black and white, 2198x2519: https://iiif.dasch.swiss/080E/39p0GV9AZiB-7HG3RtcJ3N4.jpx/full/max/0/default.png (downloaded with John's OK, 2026-10-03), aligned to the plate and used to read shapes the plate blurs; the tool does not read it.
plays.shows: The play itself. Oedipus, blind, has taken refuge at the altar in the grove at Colonus, with Antigone, who shares his exile, and Ismene, who comes with news of his sons' war and of the oracle (lines 310-509). Taplin (Pots & Plays no. 27) argues that the scene can be read only by someone who knows Sophocles' play: the story belongs to Athens and was Sophocles' own, the king at left and the young man at right fit Creon and Polynices pulling Oedipus to opposite sides, and the Erinys above stands for the goddesses of the grove, on whom Oedipus calls when he curses Polynices.
plays.method: Made with PhotoCraft (tools/oedipus_colonus.py, 2026-10-10; the first tool, 2026-10-03, is in git history). Kept as approved: the frame (Taplin's plate at 4x), Green's pages and the found photo registered to it (SIFT, homography, thin-plate spline; colour-matched), the cut, the staff, the hand-placed strokes of Oedipus' face and hand, and John's traces of the daughters' faces and Antigone's hand. Every image step in PhotoCraft: the plate's crop, JPEG cleaning and enlargement, grey, channel maps, blurs, Maximum and Minimum (local contrast; a white top-hat for the headdress's ribs). The outline smoothed along its length; painted lines along their centres at their own width, breaks joined; his white hair and beard a light tone with the dark marks between the curls as crisp strokes, no black outline; the daughters' dark hair two firm tones; Ismene's headdress black with its white ribs clear; the robe's lines kept up to the beard; the hand-placed strokes drawn at twice the frame so the faces stay crisp. Washes as paths of class tone; potrace.
plays.result: Redrawn with PhotoCraft 2026-10-10 and approved by John after three passes. Pass 1 was plainly not better (the hair worse); his asks after it: 'Iterate the hair'; 'faces need to be crisper (especially daughter or left)'; 'Oedipus's hair and beard are good but it looks like we lost lines of the clothing near the hair and beard'; Ismene's headdress drawn as attire.

plays.title: Alcestis
plays.proposed_subject: Apollo with a bull and a palm; Admetus on his horse (John's pick, 2026-10-05: sweep 2 code 11n, 'as proposed (Apollo; Admetus on his horse)'). Two drawings, which can be laid back together (John, 2026-10-07).
plays.credit: After the plate in C. Lenormant and J. de Witte, Élite des monuments céramographiques II (Paris, 1857), pl. LIV (text pp. 160-161): a red-figure neck-amphora made in Campania (the Owl-Pillar Group), formerly in the Blacas collection; London, British Museum 1867,0508.1122. The plate is signed A. Rey, sc., and Lith. de Bineteau. Scan: Heidelberg University Library.
plays.license: Public domain (published 1857). Heidelberg labels the scan with the Public Domain Mark 1.0 (the volume's IIIF manifest, checked 2026-10-07). A photograph of the vase (ArchaiOptix, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0) was only compared, not traced, so its licence does not carry over (John, 2026-10-07).
plays.crop: Two drawings from one plate, each group whole: Apollo with the palm and the bull (alcestis-apollo.svg), Admetus on his horse (alcestis-admetus.svg). Nothing joins the groups (the bull's muzzle and the horse's are about 70 px apart on the plate), so they part along the ground between them, and laid side by side at their places on the plate they give the whole scene. Left out: the black ground and the panel's edges. Drawn from Heidelberg's copy, which shows the bull's head; the Getty copy on the Internet Archive (gri_33125009347440, leaves 637-638) loses it in the binding.
alt_text: Apollo with a palm and a bull
plays.shows: Related to the play: its backstory. Apollo served Admetus as his herdsman (the prologue, lines 1-9); here he stands by a bull, and Admetus rides. The names are Panofka's and the Élite's (pp. 160-161); the British Museum's record keeps them, Apollo with a query.
plays.method: Coloured plate, red figures on black, printed across two facing pages and scanned by Heidelberg as one opening. The scan is levelled first: the frame's top and bottom edges, printed straight, made straight and level column by column; each page's tilt taken out; near the fold each column widened by the height it lost and by an estimate of how far the page sloped away from the camera, set so the dots on the bull's forehead come out round (John chose it over two narrower estimates, 'still too smooshed'); the crease painted out. A photograph of the vase (ArchaiOptix, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0) was looked at for the bull's head; nothing was traced from it. Then as Suppliant Women: the black ground gives the outline, the plate's own lines by local contrast, the faces from the plate's paint at its own width (eyes kept fine, at John's ask), the hair solid; the outline thinner on thin parts, so they keep their clay on the dark theme; the plate's own line weight; potrace. tools/alcestis.py.
plays.result: Approved by John, 2026-10-07 ('Approved'), after his rulings: Heidelberg's scan over the Getty copy, two drawings that can be laid back together, the fold flattened, the widening at the camera's 1 m. About three hours' work, most of it on the fold.

plays.author: euripides
plays.title: Andromache
plays.proposed_subject: Neoptolemos killing old Priam on the altar, the dead Astyanax across his knees (John's pick, 2026-10-05: sweep 2 code 14n, 'as proposed').
plays.credit: After Karl Reichhold's drawing in A. Furtwängler and K. Reichhold, Griechische Vasenmalerei I (Munich, 1904), Taf. 34, 'Hydria mit Iliupersis, Neapel' (text pp. 182-187): the Vivenzio hydria, a red-figure hydria by the Kleophrades Painter, from Nola; Naples, Museo Archeologico Nazionale 81669 (Heydemann 2422). Scan: Heidelberg University Library.
plays.license: Public domain (published 1904). Heidelberg labels the scan with the Public Domain Mark (page 0059, the plate from its first copy, checked 2026-10-06).
plays.crop: Neoptolemos, Priam on the altar and the dead Astyanax across his knees, whole, with the altar. Left out: the band round the vase's neck, but for Neoptolemos' crest, which overlaps it; past the blade's edges at the sword's tip, a hand and a woman's head from the scene above; the palm behind Priam (its crown is half hidden by another warrior's arm and spear, so it could not be drawn whole without inventing fronds), with the warrior and the mourning woman beyond it; the dead Trojan on his shield under Neoptolemos' legs (the legs are drawn whole over him), with the kneeling Greek who touches the group only through him, and the fallen man's hair under Priam's feet; the step under the altar. The black ground the group closes in stays open.
plays.alt_text: Neoptolemos, sword raised, kills old Priam on the altar, the dead Astyanax across his knees
plays.shows: Related to the play: the sack of Troy. Neoptolemos, Andromache's master in the play, kills Priam on the altar; the dead child is Astyanax, her son by Hector. The play's backstory, not its action.
plays.method: Printed plate, black lines on grey-brown paper, the vase's black ground printed as a dark halftone, which gives most of the outline; where the frieze's figures touch, cut along the plate's own lines (the neck band but for the crest, the sword's tip, the palm, the fallen Trojan with the legs kept whole over him, the altar's step). The plate's black lines cleared of grain by non-local means and redrawn along their centres at 0.11% of the longer side (finer than the house weight, at which close lines ran together: John chose the finer weight twice), wide black (hair, helmet, crest beads) solid; faint brown lines by a ridge filter, along their centres. Where the lines did not come clean John traced over the plate: the three faces, the hands, Priam's feet, the pleats through the blood on Priam's chest, the kilt, and lines the drawing still missed; his traces registered to the plate by SIFT. The blood is a wash in the line colour (opacity 0.25-0.55, following the plate's darkness), with the lines black through it (John's rulings). Traced as drawn (linework weight 'drawn'); potrace. tools/andromache.py, tools/andromache_traces.json.
plays.result: Approved by John, 2026-10-06 ('Approved'), after his traces of the faces, hands, feet and kilt and his rulings on the line weight and the blood. About ten hours' work (10:38-15:31 and 18:02-23:07), most of it on his traces and the blood.

plays.title: Hecuba

XVI; 2026-10-10: the pair with the tomb and the shade, drawn with PhotoCraft).
plays.credit: After the plate in E. Gerhard, Trinkschalen und Gefässe des Königlichen Museums zu Berlin II (Berlin, 1850), Taf. XVI, 'Tod der Polyxena' (text p. 32): an Attic black-figure hydria of the Leagros Group, c. 525-475 BC, from Etruria, bought by Gerhard in 1841; Berlin, Antikensammlung F 1902 (Furtwängler 1885, no. 1902). Scan: Heidelberg University Library.
plays.license: Public domain (published 1850). Heidelberg labels the scan with the Public Domain Mark 1.0 (the volume's IIIF manifest, checked 2026-10-10).
plays.crop: Polyxena, Neoptolemos with his spear, the white tomb with the snake and the animal at its foot, and Achilles' winged shade above it. Left out: the hoplite at the left with his shield and spears (cut along Polyxena's own outline; the strip of her dress that hangs over his shield's rim kept, John), the chariot of the frieze above, the frame and the ground line.
plays.alt_text: A helmeted warrior with a spear leads a veiled woman by the wrist towards a white tomb, a snake rising from the tomb and a small animal at its foot, a winged armed figure flying above

Kept: both ends of her starred shawl, its lower edge and its black folds. Left out: Apollo (his shin lines, which the old cut took in, and the ground beside them), his cloak, the laver, the Fury. Apollo's raised back foot lies across her hem: its lines are erased, and her dress's black stripe is drawn on across the gap (a straight continuation of its last 40 px); the rest of the hem there is left plain. That one line is a reconstruction.
playwrights.alt_text: The Pythia, Apollo's priestess, fleeing in terror with her hands raised
playwrights.shows: Related to the play: Orestes at Delphi, the setting of the Eumenides' opening, where the Pythia comes out of the temple in terror (34 ff.). playwrights.method: Cut by a least-cost path on the Eumenides drawing's lines; her body is her own clay inside the cut and the lines bordering it; the same printed line (1.2 scan px); potrace. tools/eumenides.py (tools/pythia.py retired).
playwrights.result: Approved by John 2026-10-12 (replace). The 2026-10-02 decisions kept (arm, head curl, fingers, the whole shawl, the stripe drawn on). The Commons copy of this plate is a blurred 1.5x upscale of the same scan; use the Heidelberg file.

playwrights.proposed_subject: The shepherd Euphorbos carrying the infant Oedipus (John, 2026-10-02)
playwrights.status: Drawn 2026-10-02 (second session); redrawn after John's review. John, 2026-10-02, on the second round: 'You flattened it right to my eyes'
playwrights.credit: After the Attic red-figure neck-amphora by the Achilles Painter, c. 450-445 BCE, from Vulci, Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, Cabinet des médailles 372 (ARV² 987.4; BAPD 213824), side A: Euphorbos carrying the infant Oedipus, both named on the vase (ΕΥΦΟΡΒΟΣ, ΟΙΔΙΠΟΔΑΣ). Photographs: ArchaiOptix, 2023 (Commons files _01 to _04). Drawing traced from the photographs and changed.
playwrights.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (all four photos by ArchaiOptix; Commons file pages checked 2026-10-02). The drawing is a derivative and is released under CC BY-SA 4.0 with this credit. The file pages add that some museums permit photography for non-commercial use only; that is a note, not a licence term.
playwrights.crop: Euphorbos with the child, his spear at full length (John, 2026-10-02: first shortened, then 'longer spear please', then full length). The meander band he stands on is cut away along his soles; the inscriptions are left out. Above his belt the figure comes from photo 03, a close view from above that looks almost straight at his head; below, from photo 02, which faces him. Past his outline the spear is drawn straight, on one line fitted to the painted shaft on both sides of him, out to its butt spike (from photo 01) and blade (from photo 04), at the lengths the vase model gives. The back of his neck, which the vase leaves unmarked, is drawn in.
playwrights.alt_text: The shepherd Euphorbos carrying the infant Oedipus on his shoulder, a long spear in his hand
playwrights.shows: Backstory the play turns on: a shepherd, named Euphorbos on the vase, carrying the infant Oedipus, the rescue that the play's last revelation brings to light. Not a scene staged in the play. Chosen by John, 2026-10-02, as Sophocles' home-page figure.
playwrights.method: Four photographs, one drawing. The vase and the four cameras fitted together (tools/vase_unroll.py: a surface of revolution and pinhole cameras, from the silhouettes, the meander's lower edge, the ring at the base of the neck, and points matched between the photos; every photo's focal length fixed from its EXIF, the cropped photos' centres fitted). The vase then flattened as rigidly as it allows, so every small patch keeps its shape. Above the belt the drawing comes from photo 03, which looks almost straight at the shoulder where his head is; below, from photo 02. Clay found by colour; painted lines by local contrast, redrawn as even lines at the house weight; the hand, the two faces and the left sandal drawn as hand-placed strokes snapped to the painted lines, the faces at a finer pen; hair and the cord on his back solid. The back of his neck drawn in where the vase has no line. tools/euphorbos.py.
playwrights.result: Two rounds on 2026-10-02; John on the second: 'You flattened it right to my eyes.' First: photo 02 unrolled by arc length; John found the head and upper body squashed ('like a Neanderthal') and the hat on his back growing out of his neck ('an insane tumor'). Cause: that unrolling shears whatever lies off its centre line where the vase's profile slopes (his face by about 8 degrees, the hat by 18), and the cameras' focal lengths had been fitted at twice their true value. Second: the shear-free flattening, the true focal lengths, the upper body from photo 03, and a line for the back of his neck (John asked for it). The head now matches photo 03, the view John pointed to, at matched scale. Open: the spear is drawn straight through his fist, though unrolled the painted shaft bends a few degrees there; a heavy dark wedge where his jaw meets the child's head; a faint clay fringe along long straight edges in dark mode comes from the shared tracer and is flagged separately.
playwrights.superseded: docs/redesign/drawings/sophocles-oedipus.svg (Oedipus before the Sphinx, Berlin F 2355, photo by Gary Todd, CC0): the phase 1 test. John found it too sparse, and the Sphinx scene misleading about the plot.

Jaene's Kunst-Anst. in Berlin') of the Duke of Buckingham's vase, Archäologische Zeitung 7 (1849), Denkmäler und Forschungen, Taf. XII ('Iphigenia in Tauris. playwrights.crop: Iphigenia with the whole tablet, the temple key, its chain and knob, and her right forearm down its outer edge. Left out: Pylades, the temple door and steps behind her (the cut follows her veil's curve, not the door's straight edge), Artemis' foot, the attendant and her tray. At this scan's size Pylades' fingertips on the tablet's far edge cannot be told apart from it, so a few strokes there may be his.
playwrights.alt_text: Iphigenia, priestess of Artemis, holding out a letter tablet and the temple key
playwrights.shows: The play itself, as O. Jahn identifies the scene in the 1849 publication: Iphigenia handing her letter to Pylades (Iphigenia in Tauris 727 ff.). Jahn records that Welcker read it the other way round, with Iphigenia receiving the letter. The vase's present location was not checked.
playwrights.method: Lithograph: fine grey lines found by local contrast with hysteresis (ink_lines); least-cost cut; house line weight; potrace. tools/iphigenia_tauris.py.
playwrights.result: Clean. Revised twice on 2026-10-02 after John's review: her right forearm, key hand, chain, sandals, veil edge and the whole tablet are in.

drawing_format: Each SVG is 1000 units tall with two paths: 'lines' (fill currentColor) and 'body', the figure's area under the lines, class "body" with fill="none", which a page fills with CSS. The body has no holes, except where a scene shows the black ground through it (Philoctetes: between his arms and his body), and lines too thin to hold clay on either side (a goad, a spear) get a narrow clay rim, so the figure reads whole on a dark page. Light pages leave the body transparent; the contact sheet's dark boards fill it with clay and keep the lines dark, as on a red-figure vase (approved by John 2026-10-02; the inverted dark mode looked like a photo negative).
